topic: Why Spain and France are stranger than you think, built around Pheasant Island
hook: Your calendar decides who owns Pheasant Island, because Spain and France swap this tiny island between them every six months.
title: Spain and France Swap This Island Every 6 Months
description:
Spain and France share a tiny island in a river, and it changes country every six months. This video counts through six true facts about Spain, France and the places between them, from a clock stuck on Berlin time to a town trapped inside France, ending on the island itself. Every fact is real and you can find each place on a map.

#geography #borders #spain
tags: why Spain time zone is wrong
comment_prompt: Which of the six would you visit first?

scenes.narration: Your calendar decides who owns Pheasant Island, because Spain and France swap this tiny island between them every six months.
scenes.headline: An Island Two Countries Share

scenes.narration: That is real, it is on the map, and nobody lives there. By the end, you will see exactly how it works.
scenes.headline: Real, Not Fake

scenes.narration: But first, five other facts about Spain and France that sound fake and are true, each one stranger than the one before.
scenes.headline: Five Facts First

scenes.narration: We start with a clock that is wrong, then a Spanish town trapped inside France, and a rock full of wild monkeys.
scenes.headline: Clock, Town, Monkey Rock

scenes.narration: After that come two Spanish cities in Africa, and a country ruled by a French president and a Spanish bishop.
scenes.headline: Cities In Africa
scenes.sub: Plus a country with two princes

scenes.narration: Stay till the end, because the island is the one that breaks every rule you know about maps.
scenes.headline: The Island Comes Last

scenes.narration: Fact one: Spain's clocks are wrong, and they have been wrong for more than eighty years, ever since 1940.
scenes.headline: Spain's Wrong Clock

scenes.narration: Find Madrid on a map and you will see it sits slightly west of London, further out into the Atlantic.
scenes.headline: Madrid Is West Of London

scenes.narration: Yet Spain's clocks run one hour ahead of London, the same time as Paris, Berlin and Warsaw, far to the east.
scenes.headline: One Hour Ahead

scenes.narration: In 1940, the dictator Francisco Franco moved Spain's clocks forward by one hour, to match the time in Nazi Germany.
scenes.headline: Franco Changed The Clock

scenes.narration: Nobody ever moved them back, so Spain still lives on Berlin time, even though the sun does not agree.
scenes.headline: Still On Berlin Time

scenes.narration: In midsummer, the sun sets after nine at night in Madrid, and even later in the far northwest of the country.
scenes.headline: Sunset After 9 PM

scenes.narration: That is one reason lunch in Spain happens around two or three, and dinner often starts at nine or ten.
scenes.headline: Late Lunch, Late Dinner

scenes.narration: A wrong clock is odd, but it is only a warm-up. The next place is a whole town standing in the wrong country.
scenes.headline: Next: A Trapped Town

scenes.narration: Fact two: Llívia is a Spanish town that sits completely inside France, with French land on every single side.
scenes.headline: Llívia, Spain Inside France

scenes.narration: Look at the map and you see a small Spanish patch, floating in the middle of France, high in the Pyrenees.
scenes.headline: A Spanish Patch In France

scenes.narration: The reason goes back to 1659, when Spain and France finally signed a peace treaty after a very long war.
scenes.headline: The Treaty Of 1659

scenes.narration: In that treaty, Spain handed over a group of villages in the Pyrenees mountains to France, to settle the border.
scenes.headline: Villages Given To France

scenes.narration: But Llívia was officially a town, not a village, so the exact wording of the treaty left it with Spain.
scenes.headline: Town, Not Village

scenes.narration: A short road now joins Llívia to the Spanish town of Puigcerdà, but that road runs across French land.
scenes.headline: A Road Through France

scenes.narration: So a single word in an old treaty still decides which country a whole town belongs to today.
scenes.headline: One Word, One Town

scenes.narration: Remember that treaty from 1659, because it comes back at the end, and it created the biggest surprise of all.
scenes.headline: Remember 1659

scenes.narration: But next, we go to the southern tip of Spain, where a huge rock is not Spanish at all.
scenes.headline: Next: A Rock Not Spanish

scenes.narration: Fact three: at the very southern edge of Spain, there is a piece of Britain, and it is called Gibraltar.
scenes.headline: Gibraltar: A Piece Of Britain

scenes.narration: It has been British since a treaty signed in 1713, and Spain has claimed it back ever since.
scenes.headline: British Since 1713

scenes.narration: Even so, people walk across the land border between Gibraltar and Spain all the time, to work, to shop and to visit.
scenes.headline: Walk Between Two Countries

scenes.narration: At the top of the huge rock live Barbary macaques, which are the only wild monkeys living anywhere in Europe.
scenes.headline: Europe's Only Wild Monkeys

scenes.narration: So Europe's only wild monkeys live on a British rock, attached to Spain, looking out across the sea at Africa.
scenes.headline: British Rock, Spanish Coast

scenes.narration: And speaking of Africa, Spain has something even more surprising there, whole cities that count as part of Spain and Europe.
scenes.headline: Next: Spain In Africa

scenes.narration: Fact four: Spain owns two cities on the African continent, called Ceuta and Melilla, both on the coast of Morocco.
scenes.headline: Ceuta And Melilla

scenes.narration: They are not colonies. They are Spanish cities, with Spanish passports, the euro, and the rules of the European Union.
scenes.headline: Spanish Passports, Euros

scenes.narration: That means the European Union has land borders with Africa, and these two cities are the only places where it happens.
scenes.headline: EU Land Border With Africa

scenes.narration: Tall fences mark those borders, so you can stand in a city that is in Europe's club while looking at Morocco.
scenes.headline: Fences At The Border

scenes.narration: Ceuta even looks across the narrow strait at Gibraltar, so European-run land sits on both shores of that water.
scenes.headline: Europe On Both Shores

scenes.narration: Morocco also claims these cities, so the border here is a live argument, not just a line on a map.
scenes.headline: A Border Still Argued

scenes.narration: So far we have a clock, a trapped town, a monkey rock and two cities in Africa, and it keeps getting stranger.
scenes.headline: It Keeps Getting Stranger

scenes.narration: If you like strange maps and strange facts like these, subscribe, because there are many more places to come.
scenes.headline: Subscribe For More

scenes.narration: Now the next fact has a country with two leaders, and neither of them is actually from that country.
scenes.headline: Two Leaders, Neither Local

scenes.narration: Fact five: Andorra, a tiny country in the mountains between France and Spain, has two heads of state at the same time.
scenes.headline: Andorra's Two Princes

scenes.narration: One is the Bishop of Urgell, a Catholic bishop who lives in Spain. The other is the President of France.
scenes.headline: A Bishop And A President

scenes.narration: Yes, the president of France is also, officially, a prince of another country. He gets that job just by being president.
scenes.headline: France's President Is A Prince

scenes.narration: The deal goes back to 1278, when a French count and a Spanish bishop argued over who ruled the Andorran valleys.
scenes.headline: The Deal From 1278

scenes.narration: Instead of fighting it out, they signed an agreement to share the land, and that sharing never really ended.
scenes.headline: They Chose To Share

scenes.narration: Today the two princes mostly have a ceremonial role, and Andorra's own government runs daily life in the country.
scenes.headline: Ceremonial Princes

scenes.narration: Andorra is not in the European Union, yet it uses the euro, which makes its status even more unusual.
scenes.headline: Not In The EU, Uses Euros

scenes.narration: Sharing a country between two rulers is strange, but sharing one island by the calendar is stranger, and that is next.
scenes.headline: Next: The Island

scenes.narration: Fact six: Pheasant Island, the one we promised you. Your calendar decides who owns it, and the rules are strict.
scenes.headline: Pheasant Island

scenes.narration: It sits in the Bidasoa river, which forms part of the border, with the Spanish town of Irun on one bank.
scenes.headline: In The Bidasoa River

scenes.narration: On the other bank is the French town of Hendaye, so the island floats right between two countries and two languages.
scenes.headline: Hendaye On The Other Side

scenes.narration: It is only about two hundred metres long and about forty metres across, which is smaller than many city parks.
scenes.headline: Tiny: 200 By 40 Metres

scenes.narration: Nobody lives there, and the island is closed to the public, so there are no houses, shops or tourist boats.
scenes.headline: Closed To The Public

scenes.narration: From the first of February to the thirty-first of July, the island belongs to Spain, and Spain looks after it.
scenes.headline: Feb To July: Spain

scenes.narration: From the first of August to the thirty-first of January, it belongs to France instead, and France takes over.
scenes.headline: Aug To Jan: France

scenes.narration: So it is Spanish for six months, French for six months, and it changes country twice every year without any fight.
scenes.headline: Two Switches Every Year

scenes.narration: The story starts in 1659. Spain and France had been at war for about twenty-four years, and both sides were exhausted.
scenes.headline: A War Of 24 Years

scenes.narration: They needed a meeting place that felt fair to both, so they picked this little island in the middle of the river.
scenes.headline: A Fair Meeting Place

scenes.narration: There, the two sides negotiated the Treaty of the Pyrenees, the same treaty that left Llívia inside France.
scenes.headline: The Same Treaty As Llívia
scenes.visual_query: Treaty of Pyrenees Pheasant Island painting

scenes.narration: The peace was sealed with a royal marriage, and in 1660 the kings of Spain and France met on this island.
scenes.headline: Two Kings Met Here

scenes.narration: The Spanish king's famous court painter, Diego Velázquez, helped organise the royal trip, and he died not long after returning home.
scenes.headline: Velázquez Was There

scenes.narration: Even earlier, in 1526, the French king Francis the First was freed on this river, in exchange for his two sons.
scenes.headline: A King Swapped For Sons

scenes.narration: So this small island has seen kings, hostages and royal brides cross it, long before it became a quiet river rock.
scenes.headline: Kings, Hostages, Brides

scenes.narration: Even today, the island has a governor, and the job goes to a naval officer from whichever country holds the island.
scenes.headline: Governed By A Naval Officer

scenes.narration: While the island is Spanish, a Spanish naval officer is in charge. When it turns French, a French one takes over.
scenes.headline: The Governor Switches Too

scenes.narration: There is no wall on it and no fight over it, only a calendar that two old rivals have followed for centuries.
scenes.headline: No Wall, Just A Calendar

scenes.narration: Think about that. Two countries that fought for decades settled their peace on a tiny island, and the sharing has lasted ever since.
scenes.headline: From War To Sharing

scenes.narration: You cannot visit, but from the riverbank you can see it, a small green island, with two nations quietly taking turns.
scenes.headline: Visible From The Riverbank

scenes.narration: So on any day of the year, you can tell who owns Pheasant Island, just by checking which month it is.
scenes.headline: Check The Month

scenes.narration: Let us run through them again: a clock stuck on Berlin time, and a Spanish town trapped inside France.
scenes.headline: Quick Recap

scenes.narration: A British rock with wild monkeys, two Spanish cities in Africa, and a country with a French president as its prince.
scenes.headline: Rock, Cities, Princes

scenes.narration: And one island that is Spanish for six months, then French for six months, then Spanish again.
scenes.headline: Spanish, French, Spanish

scenes.narration: So remember, your calendar decides who owns Pheasant Island, and it has done so since 1659.
scenes.headline: Your Calendar Decides

scenes.narration: Next in this series: another country that looks perfectly normal on the map, and is not.
scenes.headline: Next In The Series
